objective: Design dashboards: panels that match the metric type, rate windows, units, legends, variables and avoiding misleading aggregations
secondaryObjectives: Alerting basics: when to alert (symptoms over causes), what to alert on (SLO burn, saturation that predicts impact) and why pages must be actionable
Configuring alerting rules: alert, expr, for, labels and annotations with templating, rule groups and evaluation interval

Read 2026-11-17 with WebFetch (a summarizing fetch) of the primary page, found by WebSearch. Confirms: summary quantiles cannot be aggregated and averaging quantiles is statistically nonsensical; histograms aggregate with histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(..._bucket[5m]))); for a 300 ms objective use buckets around 300 ms; the share of requests within 300 ms comes from the le=0.3 bucket over the count.

Read 2026-11-17 with WebFetch (a summarizing fetch) of the primary page, found by WebSearch. Confirms: $__rate_interval is max($__interval + scrape interval, 4 x scrape interval) and is recommended for rate and increase, so the window is always at least four times the scrape interval.

sources.cite: Google SRE Workbook, chapter 5: Alerting on SLOs
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 with WebFetch (a summarizing fetch) of the primary page, found by WebSearch. Confirms: multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerts: page on 2% of the budget in 1 hour (5-minute short window, burn rate 14.4) and 5% in 6 hours (30-minute short window), ticket on slower burns; the short window, 1/12 of the long one, lets the alert reset soon after errors stop.

The company, the services, the metrics and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You own monitoring for checkout at Marigold Shoes, a fictional online shoe store. Last night checkout was slow for 40 minutes; the latency panel stayed flat and the on-call engineer was paged three times for CPU on a batch node instead. The checkout SLO: 99% of requests under 300 ms over 30 days.
handover: Scrape interval 30s. The latency panel shows avg(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_sum[1m])) / avg(rate(..._count[1m])) across all instances.
The only page is an alert on node CPU above 80% for 1 minute.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the map shows each component and its status in words.
Move on a check-in at a time. A decision comes to you at each check-in; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Check-in 2: a repeat of last night's slowdown on one instance shows as a 40 ms bump on the new panel; nobody reacts.
Check-in 3: Prometheus falls behind on ingestion and drops samples; rule evaluations time out and dashboards lag by minutes.
Check-in 4: on-call is paged eleven times overnight for batch CPU and mutes the channel; a real checkout slowdown at 03:00 goes unseen.

quantPrompt.title: A flat line during an outage
quantPrompt.context: The panel averages averages; the metric is a histogram.

choices.label: Plot histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[2m]))) in seconds, plus a per-instance variable to break it down

effects.log: The panel now shows p99, with a per-instance view.

choices.feedback: Quantiles come from bucket rates summed by le first; averaging hides exactly the tail customers feel.

choices.label: Switch to the maximum of per-instance averages

effects.log: The panel shows the worst instance's average.

choices.feedback: The bad instance shows, but an average still hides the tail.

choices.label: Compute p99 per instance with histogram_quantile and average those p99s
choices.feedback: Averaging quantiles is mathematically meaningless; one bad instance among twelve is diluted to a small bump.

choices.label: Use the dashboard's rate-interval variable (at least four times the scrape interval, so 2m here) in every rate panel

effects.log: Rate panels use a 2-minute or longer window.

choices.feedback: A rate needs at least two samples in the window; four scrape intervals leaves room for a missed scrape.

choices.label: Switch to irate over 1m
choices.feedback: irate draws lines from the last two samples, but is jumpy and still gaps when a scrape is missed.

choices.label: Scrape every service every 1 second so 1-minute windows fill
choices.feedback: Thirty times the samples overloads Prometheus and the targets for no gain in the dashboards' accuracy.

pagePrompt.title: Paged for CPU, not for customers
pagePrompt.context: The SLO: 99% of requests under 300 ms over 30 days.

choices.label: Add multiwindow burn-rate alerts on the share of requests over 300 ms (fast: 1h and 5m windows; slow: 6h and 30m), with for, severity labels and a runbook link; turn NodeCPUHigh into a ticket

effects.log: Burn-rate pages; CPU becomes a ticket.

choices.feedback: Page on the symptom customers feel, at a rate that will spend the error budget; causes such as CPU go to tickets.

choices.label: Add an alert on p99 above 300 ms for 5 minutes, and keep the CPU page

effects.log: A p99 threshold alert is added.

choices.feedback: It catches big slowdowns, but pages on short blips, and CPU still wakes people for nothing.

choices.label: Lower the CPU alert to 60% so it pages earlier
choices.feedback: More pages about a cause that doesn't affect customers, and still none about latency.

parts.label: Dashboard

scoring.modelReasoning: Dashboards must match the metric type: latency is a histogram, so quantiles come from histogram_quantile over bucket rates summed by le; averaging averages or quantiles hides the tail and the bad instance. A rate window needs several samples, at least four scrape intervals. Pages should be actionable and about symptoms: multiwindow burn-rate alerts on the SLO page when the error budget is burning; causes like CPU belong in tickets.
